## How This Relates to IFS

Richard Schwartz started [Internal Family Systems](https://ifs-institute.com/) (IFS) back in the 1980s. This method overlaps with it a lot. IFS recognizes protective parts too, and teaches people to approach them without shame or a fight, so "meet the protector first" fits right in. My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. In standard IFS, the healer is the Self, a calm, compassionate source that's supposed to show up once your parts "unblend." I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru.

And what if that calm inner source just won't show up for you? That's where borrowed adulthood comes in. Maybe you borrow one grown-up job from a friend, or from a plan you've made, and take it in bit by bit. I have no use for another neo-Advaita, [spiritual-bypassing](http://goenka.u-dont-exist.com/) claim that a perfect Higher Self is already waiting underneath everything. A grown-up you can trust gets built through care and boundaries, and through action and direction.

IFS calls these wounded young parts "exiles." I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition. IFS "unburdening," often done after witnessing a part's origin story, can be powerful. But it can also get dramatic, with a lot of focus on memories and plenty of room for suggestion, and that can knock people off balance, especially if they tend to dissociate (DID-like fragmentation included) or to spiritually bypass.

And then there's the map itself. Managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... how many parts is that now? It can turn into a maze. Some practitioners use the model gently, and others seem to leave people more fragmented while trying to fix the fragmenting. Having institutes and certifications behind a framework doesn't make it any more true, or safer for that matter.

Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of IFS and reparenting. Could an IFS therapist help? They may, if they're skilled and grounded. You'd want one who's trauma-informed and doesn't put ideas in your head, especially one who understands dissociation. For your little one's pain, or for shame, a good reparenting therapist may fit better. The same goes for attachment wounds or abandoning yourself, or not having an inner adult you can count on.

### Related Clinical Work

This framework grew out of my own practice, plus the teachers and collaborators I credit below. Later revisions also compare notes with other approaches, like schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy, spiritually integrated psychotherapy and so on. Those don't even agree with each other on everything! So I borrow particular ideas and practices from them, and that's it. I'm not saying they'd sign off on the whole synthesis, or that their research proves it as a package.
